props.title: D.O.A.
props.initialSlug: Dying to solve his own murder.

sections.content: D.O.A. revolutionized noir storytelling with its killer premise: an accountant discovers he's been fatally poisoned and has just days to solve his own murder. The film's opening sequence - Frank Bigelow stumbling into a police station to report "I want to file a murder report... I was murdered" - ranks among noir's most gripping hooks. Director Rudolph Maté, who shot masterpieces like Carl Theodor Dreyer's The Passion of Joan of Arc (1928), brings his cinematographer's eye to the shadows and angles of San Francisco and Los Angeles. This influenced later "racing against time" thrillers like Speed (1994) and Crank (2006).

sections.content: D.O.A.'s influence extends beyond noir into modern thrillers about protagonists racing against death. Memento (2000) borrowed its "dying man seeking justice" premise while adding memory loss. Edge of Tomorrow (2014) and Source Code (2011) adapted the "solve your own death" concept into sci-fi territory. The film's documentary-style opening and use of real locations prefigured neo-noir classics like Chinatown (1974) and The French Connection (1971).

The film's depiction of post-war Los Angeles and San Francisco captures a transitional moment in American urban life. Like Double Indemnity (1944) and Out of the Past (1947), D.O.A. shows a darker side of California's promise. The neon-lit nightclub scenes and jazz soundtrack influenced countless later noirs, including Odds Against Tomorrow (1959) and Touch of Evil (1958). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Modern Interpretations

sections.content: D.O.A.'s premise proved so compelling it spawned multiple remakes, including Color Me Dead (1969) and Dennis Quaid's D.O.A.. Its influence appears in neo-noir classics like Point Blank (1967) and Get Carter (1971), which share its revenge-driven narrative. The film's mix of procedural investigation and existential dread echoes through contemporary thrillers like Taken (2008) and John Wick (2014).
